issues.legal_issue: A High Court, as a Court of Record, has inherent power to review its own judgment to correct an apparent error even when a statutory review provision specifies grounds for review.
material_facts: A claim for exemption from vesting was made only under one statutory exception, and the claimant presented evidence only in support of that exception.

The High Court nevertheless granted relief under a different exception, although the claimant had neither pleaded that he cultivated the land before the relevant date nor given evidence of such cultivation.
A later statutory amendment provided specified grounds for review of High Court decisions, and the High Court reviewed its earlier judgment after finding an apparent error on its face.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had inherent power, as a Court of Record, to review its own judgment for an apparent error, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. It did not decide whether the failure to raise a contention amounted to a concession under the statutory review provision.
issues.legal_principle: Article 215 of the Constitution makes the High Court a Court of Record. Such a court has plenary inherent power and a duty to keep its record correct, including by correcting an apparent error in its own judgment. The Court relied on Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar v. State of Maharashtra and M.F. Elisabeth v. Harwan Investment & Trading Pvt. Ltd. Section 8C(2) of the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971 specified grounds for review, but did not exhaust the High Court’s inherent power as a Court of Record. The Court left open whether the State counsel’s failure to raise a contention constituted a concession within that provision.

predicates.high_court_review_of_own_judgment: The proceeding asks a High Court to review its own earlier judgment.
predicates.high_court_is_court_of_record: The court whose judgment is under review is a superior court that keeps its proceedings as an authoritative record.
predicates.record_contains_apparent_error: The earlier judgment contains an error apparent from the record, such as granting relief on a ground that was neither claimed nor supported by evidence.
predicates.high_court_may_review_own_judgment_to_co: The High Court may review its own judgment to correct an apparent error.

issues.definition: When a High Court is reviewing its own judgment and the record shows an apparent error, its status as a Court of Record permits it to correct that error.
